summary: This RFC describes the Network Time Protocol, which synchronizes network clocks with distributed clients and servers over UDP. It evolved from the Time Protocol and ICMP Timestamp message. This early version was replaced by RFC 1059, RFC 1119, and RFC 1305.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers across the world check with each other so they all agree what time it is, like friends comparing watches.

questions: what is the network time protocol
how are timestamps represented in ntp
subtitle: Synchronize network clocks using distributed clients and servers.

tldr.problem: Computers need to maintain synchronized time across networks for coordinating events and detecting anomalies, but they drift and need periodic correction.
tldr.mechanism: NTP lets distributed clients and servers compare their local clocks by exchanging messages containing timestamps. Each peer calculates the roundtrip delay and clock offset, then selects the best reference clock to synchronize its own time.
tldr.outcome: This version of NTP (version 0) was replaced by RFC 1059, RFC 1119, and RFC 1305, which provided improved synchronization algorithms and formats.

today: RFC 958 is an early version of the Network Time Protocol published in September 1985. This version was superseded by RFC 1059, RFC 1119, and RFC 1305, which provided improved and more thoroughly specified protocols.

sections.title: Introduction to Network Time Protocol
sections.content:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) is a protocol for synchronizing a set of network clocks using distributed clients and servers. It is built on the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which provides a connectionless transport mechanism. NTP evolved from the Time Protocol and the ICMP Timestamp message and provides a replacement for both.

NTP provides protocol mechanisms to synchronize time to precisions in the order of nanoseconds while preserving a non-ambiguous date. The protocol specifies data representation and message formats but does not specify the synchronizing algorithms or filtering mechanisms themselves. Each peer can determine the timekeeping characteristics of its peers, including expected clock accuracies, and select the best time from multiple sources to update its local clock.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP lets computers on a network ask each other what time it is and adjust their clocks based on the answers. It is not just one program asking a time server, but many computers checking with each other to agree on the correct time.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Service Model
sections.content:
The service model describes how NTP organizes network clocks into a hierarchical structure. Primary reference clocks are synchronized by wire or radio to national standards and connected to centrally accessible resources such as gateways. These gateways use NTP to cross-check the primary clocks and mitigate errors due to equipment or propagation failures. Secondary reference clocks (local-net hosts) run NTP with one or more gateways and redistribute time to other hosts on their local network.

The protocol does not specify algorithms for organizing this hierarchy; that is left for further study. The hierarchy can be organized based on clock precision or estimated error, and information from NTP can serve as a rudimentary routing algorithm to organize the subnetwork itself.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP clocks are organized like a pyramid: accurate clocks at the top synchronize with less accurate ones below. Each computer passes the correct time down the chain so everyone ends up with nearly the same time.

sections.title: Protocol Modes and Message Exchange
sections.content:
NTP operates in two modes: unsymmetric and symmetric. In the most common unsymmetric mode, a client sends an NTP message to one or more servers and processes the replies. The server simply interchanges addresses and ports, fills in or overwrites certain fields in the message, and returns it immediately. Servers in unsymmetric mode need not retain any state information between client requests.

In symmetric mode, the client-server distinction disappears. Each peer maintains a table of active peers with status information and copies of the Originate Timestamp and Receive Timestamp values last received from each peer. The peer periodically sends an NTP message to each peer, and the interval between messages is managed solely by the sending peer.

The mode is determined by inspecting the UDP Source Port and Destination Port fields. If both contain the NTP service port number 123, the peer is operating in symmetric mode. If they differ and the destination port contains 123, it is a client request. If the source port contains 123, it is a server reply.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP can work two ways. In the simple way, a computer asks a time server and gets an answer. In the fancier way, computers keep talking with each other, constantly checking and updating their understanding of the correct time.

sections.title: Timestamp Format and Message Fields
sections.content:
NTP timestamps are represented as a 64-bit fixed-point number in seconds relative to 0000 UT on 1 January 1900. The integer part occupies the first 32 bits and the fraction part the last 32 bits. This format allows convenient multiple-precision arithmetic and conversion to Time Protocol representation in seconds. The low-order fraction bit increments at about 0.2-nanosecond intervals, so a free-running one-millisecond clock will be in error less than one part per million, or less than a second per year.

An NTP message contains several important fields: the Leap Indicator (warning of impending leap-second), Status (indicating local clock health), Reference Clock Type (identifying the type of reference source), Precision (signed integer indicating clock precision to the nearest power of two), Estimated Error (in seconds), Estimated Drift Rate, Reference Clock Identifier, and four timestamps: Reference Timestamp (when the clock was last corrected), Originate Timestamp (when the client's request departed), Receive Timestamp (when the server received the request), and Transmit Timestamp (when the server's reply departed).
sections.plainLanguage: Each NTP message is like a timestamp journal entry where a computer writes down what time it thinks it is, what its clock is like, and when different things happened. The timestamps are very precise, measuring billionths of a second.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization and Filtering
sections.content:
The destination peer calculates the roundtrip delay (d) and clock offset (c) from the message timestamps using the formula: d = (t4 - t1) - (t3 - t2) and c = ((t2 - t1) + (t3 - t4)) / 2, where t1, t2, t3 are the Originate, Receive, and Transmit Timestamps, and t4 is the local time when the message is received. This calculation assumes the one-way delay is statistically half the roundtrip delay and that the intrinsic drift rates of both clocks are small and similar.

Clock synchronization requires long periods and multiple comparisons. While a few comparisons usually maintain time to within a second (to protect against hardware failures), maintaining time to within tens of milliseconds requires periods of hours or days and tens or hundreds of comparisons. The protocol provides flexibility in how these samples are filtered and used; the RFC does not specify the algorithms for doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: To find the right time, a computer compares messages from several sources, measuring how long they took to arrive and guessing the clock offset. The more checks it does over time, the more accurate its clock becomes.

fields.name: LI/Status/Type/Precision
fields.desc: Leap Indicator (2 bits), Status (6 bits), Reference Clock Type (8 bits), Precision (16 bits)

fields.name: Estimated Error
fields.desc: Estimated error of the local clock at time last set, in seconds.

fields.name: Estimated Drift Rate
fields.desc: Estimated drift rate of the local clock, dimensionless.

fields.name: Reference Clock Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the reference clock (ASCII string for primary, IP address for secondary).

fields.name: Reference Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when the local clock was last set or corrected.

fields.name: Originate Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when the request departed the client host.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when the request arrived at the server host.

fields.name: Transmit Timestamp
fields.desc: Time when the reply departed the server host.
